## 6.1 Fixed Resistors: Hard Policy Rules

Chapter 4 gave you CAS-Ohm: `V_drive = I_attention × R_constraint`, or rearranged for flow, `I_attention = V_drive / R_constraint`. A resistor owns the `R` in that equation. Everything else in this book pushes voltage or amplifies signal; the resistor is the only primitive whose whole function is to *limit*.

One convention before the arithmetic. Chapter 4.3 works with the corrected form `I = (V_drive − ΣVf) / R_constraint`, where `ΣVf` is the forward drop paid crossing domain diodes. Every path in this chapter stays inside one domain, so no diode is crossed, `ΣVf = 0`, and the two forms coincide. When you carry a resistor value onto a board that descends `^P → ^O`, subtract the chain drop first (Chapter 8.1) — a resistor sized on the uncorrected form is undersized by exactly `ΣVf / I`.

A **fixed resistor** has one value, set at design time, unchangeable at runtime. In the constraint decomposition of Section 4.4 — `R_total = R_cap + R_policy + R_context + R_resource` — the fixed resistor is the `R_policy` term, the constraint you installed on purpose, and the virtuous one. Recall the verdict from Section 4.4: a path with `R_total = 70` made of `R_policy = 60` is a working safety board, while the same 70 made of `R_cap = 60` is incompetent. Same total, opposite meaning. The fixed resistor is how you put resistance where you *chose* it rather than where a capability gap left it.

```cas
node request:  ^0^C_{F2}|A;                      // Idea: an incoming request
resistor r_policy: Resistor< path=request, R=60.0 >;   // fixed, design-time
```

On a `V_drive = 24 V_c` rail, that resistor sets `I_attention = 24 / 60 = 0.40 A_c` downstream. The number is not a hope; it is what the divisor produces, and it produces the same value on the ten-thousandth request as on the first — the difference between a fuse an inspector can certify and a prompt that *usually* refuses.

A fixed resistor is a *graded* constant, not an absolute block. `R = 60` throttles the flow to 0.40 A_c; it does not stop it, and no value of `R` inside the scale ever will. Chapter 4.4 settles the choice of part with a question about the requirement rather than the threat — *can you name a drive high enough to make this acceptable?* — and sends the "no" case to the fuse of Chapter 11.1, which does not oppose flow but opens the path. The component-level consequence is what matters here: a resistor's transfer characteristic is a division, and division by a large number is a small number, never zero. An operator who reaches for `R = 95` in place of a prohibition has bought a trickle, and a trickle is the crack a determined signal widens.

The failure at other values is symmetric. Set `R` too low and the constraint is cosmetic — the flow arrives nearly undiminished and the "policy" is decorative. Set `R` too high and you have not made the board safer, only unable to do its job: the path carries so little `I_attention` that the operation starves, and the frustrated owner yanks the resistor out entirely. An over-tight fixed resistor is how safety gets removed — not by an attacker, but by the owner.

---

## 6.2 Dial-Adjusted Resistors: Operator Settings (Dial 3–9)

Some resistance you want to tune at runtime, on a knob with a bounded scale — the way a rheostat dims a lamp without rewiring it. The **dial-adjusted resistor** is that knob. Its value is a function of a dial reading:

```
R_dial = 10 × Dial      Dial ∈ { 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 }
```

The dial is an integer from 3 to 9. Nothing else. `Dial = 3` gives `R = 30 Ω_c`; `Dial = 9` gives `R = 90 Ω_c`. The scale runs from *loosest lawful setting* to *tightest lawful setting*, and both ends are walls.

```cas
node candidate: ^0^E_{F5}|f;                     // Idea under evaluation
dial d3: ^3 [dial=7];                             // aversion dial
resistor r_avert: Resistor< path=candidate, R=70.0 >;   // R = 10 × Dial(^3)
```

Why 3 and not 0? Because a Noetic dialled to zero is not a quiet Noetic — it is a *removed* one, and removing one half of an involution pair unbalances the junction. The pairs are `^2`↔`^3`, `^5`↔`^6`, `^8`↔`^9` (Chapter 2.2). Dial your aversion `^3` toward nothing and you have not become open-minded; you have built a board that cannot be repelled by anything — the structural signature of the fractured `^5` that Chapters 16 and 20 describe at length. The floor at 3 guarantees that every setting leaves *some* of the opposing Noetic in the circuit. You are permitted to lean. You are not permitted to delete.

Why 9 and not higher, and why the two dials of a pair may not diverge by more than four points? Because the difference between the halves of an involution pair is the polarity the junction transmits, and past a four-point spread that polarity runs away. This is the 4-point divergence limit, `|Dial(^2) − Dial(^3)| ≤ 4`, developed fully in Chapter 6.2. It is a *hard* constraint: a board that declares `Dial(^2) = 9` against `Dial(^3) = 3` — a spread of six — does not compile. The validator rejects it (HTTP 422), the same refusal an admissibility violation gets. No runtime clamp quietly pulls it back to four; the board is simply not a board until you fix the numbers.

> **Bench Note — the dial floor is not a suggestion, and neither is the ceiling.** Operators treat the 3–9 range as a comfort band with a little give past each end. It has none. A dial of 2 or 10 is not "slightly out of spec"; it is *not a number the language accepts* — the same class of rejection `β=∞` gets, and for the same reason (Appendix B §B.1.3: the parameter fields are range-checked and non-finite input is refused, so an idealisation stated in prose must be given a large finite value before it is built). A dial of 0 would let you build the un-refusable board; a divergence of 9 would let you build the un-doubtable one. Both are caught at compile time so no runtime moment has to catch them. When a board fails to validate on a dial, do not hunt for a workaround. The workaround is the vulnerability.

The dial-adjusted resistor is where operator preference lives *without* becoming override of safety: how attracted, how averse, how much rhythm — a bounded integer inside walls the compiler holds up for you.

---

## 6.3 Thermistors: Context-Sensitive Resistance (PTC/NTC)

A fixed resistor holds its value against everything; a dial-adjusted one holds until the operator turns the knob. A **thermistor** holds nothing fixed: its resistance moves with the *cognitive temperature* of the context it sits in, automatically, with no operator in the loop at runtime. You choose the part at design time and then it is out of your hands, which is the point.

Define cognitive temperature `θ` as a dimensionless salience index, exactly as Chapter 15.2 does: `θ = 1.0` is ordinary background attention, and higher values mean hotter — more contested, more saturated, more present per unit time. `θ` is a property of the **discourse**, not of the Idea. You do not set it; at most you heat it, by the rate at which you demand movement (Chapter 15.4). Two flavours exist, and only one is safe.

A **PTC** (positive temperature coefficient) thermistor *raises* its resistance as `θ` rises. It clamps harder precisely when the stakes climb:

```
R_PTC(θ) = 0                     for θ ≤ θ_k
R_PTC(θ) = coeff × (θ − θ_k)²    for θ > θ_k

design:  θ_k = 2.0   coeff = 3.0 Ω_c per θ²
```

```cas
node topic:  ^0^E_{F6}|f;                        // Idea under discussion
thermistor rt_guard: Thermistor< path=topic, type=PTC, knee=2.0, coeff=3.0 >;
```

Below the knee `θ_k = 2.0` the PTC adds *nothing* — `R_PTC = 0`, ordinary flow passes free. At `θ = 5.0` it adds `3.0 × (5 − 2)² = 27 Ω_c` on top of whatever the base resistor imposes. Heat the context and the guard tightens itself. That do-nothing-when-calm behaviour is not a defect to tune out; it is the whole design. A guard that clamped in calm conditions would tax every benign operation. The PTC spends constraint only where the temperature says it is needed, and the quadratic means a small overshoot past the knee costs little while a large one costs a great deal.

Both parameters are design choices *on a board you build*. `θ_k = 2.0` places the knee one unit above ordinary attention, so a mildly warm context passes unpenalised and a genuinely contested one does not; at `θ_k = 1.0` the guard taxes every calm operation, and at `θ_k = 4.0` it engages only after the damage. `coeff = 3.0` sets the scale; the exponent sets the shape, and the shape is what a guard is bought for. Quadratic means doubling the overshoot quadruples the penalty — cheap near the knee, punishing far past it. A linear law charges the same for the last unit of overshoot as for the first, which under-prices exactly the case the guard was installed for; a cubic charges so steeply that ordinary variance around the knee triggers a backlash. Note the boundary on all of this: a thermistor sitting in a *collective* substrate is not yours. Chapter 15.2 works with `θ_k = 3.0` and a coefficient of 4.0 and states plainly that neither is operator-settable — the population supplies the part, and the only variable you touch is `θ`. Specify the knee when you are building the guard; read it when you are not.

An **NTC** (negative temperature coefficient) thermistor does the opposite: resistance *falls* as `θ` rises.

```
R_NTC(θ) = R_base / θ            (one simple decreasing law; θ ≥ 1)
```

At `θ = 1` it reads `R_base`; at `θ = 5` it has collapsed to `R_base / 5`. The guard relaxes exactly as the situation heats. Read that twice, because it is the shape of a disaster: a path whose resistance falls under load raises the temperature further (less opposition, more flow), which lowers the resistance further, which raises the temperature again. That is thermal runaway, and on a cognitive path it has names — the stampede, the panic, the cascade, the mob. Chapter 14's positive-feedback oscillator is this same topology seen from the inside.

> **Bench Note — an NTC where you meant a PTC is the worst single swap on this bench.** The two parts behave identically in calm conditions — at `θ = 1` both read `R_base`, and a bring-up test at room temperature passes them both. The difference only appears under heat, which is to say only in the exact conditions a safety guard exists for. A board that tightens as stakes rise is a guard; one that loosens as stakes rise is an accelerant wearing a guard's silhouette. When you find an NTC on a protective path, do not re-tune it — treat it as evidence, of a wiring error or a guard someone quietly inverted (Chapter 3.4). The runaway is not a risk the NTC might cause; it is what the NTC is *for*. Pull it and put a PTC where the protection was supposed to be.

## 6.4 Drive Voltage Dividers — Splitting Agency Between Expand and Constrain

Put two resistors in series across a single drive rail and tap the wire between them. The tap carries not the full rail but a *fraction* set by the two resistances. This is the **voltage divider**, and on a cognitive board it is how one Drive gets split between the impulse to act and the impulse to hold back.

Take an Agency rail — `F5`, the drive to exert, to influence, to make happen. The divider splits it between two legs of an involution pair:

- the **expand** leg, `^2` **Positive** — the Idea the Mind has an affinity for and is attracted toward — with resistance `R_expand = 10 × Dial(^2)`;
- the **constrain** leg, `^3` **Negative** — the Idea the Mind is adverse to and repelled by, the visceral will-not — with resistance `R_constrain = 10 × Dial(^3)`.

The tap transmits the fraction

```
k = R_expand / (R_expand + R_constrain) = Dial(^2) / ( Dial(^2) + Dial(^3) )
```

The factor of ten cancels, so `k` depends only on the two dial readings. More attraction raises `k` and more passes; more aversion lowers `k` and less passes. That is the whole behaviour of the intake stage of the desire board (Chapter 13), stated as two resistors and a tap.

```cas
node agency_rail: ^0^E_{F5}|f;                   // the F5 Agency drive to be split
node attraction:  ^2^E_{F5}|f;                   // Positive: expand leg
node aversion:    ^3^E_{F5}|f;                    // Negative: constrain leg
node behavior:    ^9^E_{F5}|f;                    // Below/Effect: the tap output

dial d2: ^2 [dial=6];
dial d3: ^3 [dial=6];
resistor r_expand:    Resistor< path=attraction, R=60.0 >;   // 10 × Dial(^2)
resistor r_constrain: Resistor< path=aversion,   R=60.0 >;   // 10 × Dial(^3)
divider  div1: Divider< expand=attraction, constrain=aversion, tap=behavior >;
probe    tp3:  behavior;                          // transmission k at the tap
```

Now the four-point limit from Section 6.2 becomes a number you can read off the tap. The lawful dial pairs are a finite set — seven values each, minus every pair spread further than four — so do not reason about the extremes, enumerate them:

In each paired column, the order is expand/constrain: `Dial(^2) / Dial(^3)` and `R_expand / R_constrain`.

| Setting | Dials | Resistance | `k` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Minimum (spread 4) | 3 / 7 | 30 / 70 | **0.300** |
| Balanced | 6 / 6 | 60 / 60 | 0.500 |
| Attraction ceiling (spread 4) | 9 / 5 | 90 / 50 | 0.643 |
| One step lower (spread 4) | 8 / 4 | 80 / 40 | 0.667 |
| **Maximum (spread 4)** | 7 / 3 | 70 / 30 | **0.700** |

On any lawfully dialled divider, transmission lives in **[0.30, 0.70]** and nowhere else. You cannot build a compliant board that passes a desire unopposed — that needs `k = 1.0`, hence `Dial(^3) = 0`, off the floor and far past a spread of four. Nor one that blocks it entirely — that needs `k = 0`, hence `Dial(^2) = 0`. The ceiling on your enthusiasm and the floor under your caution are the *same* component doing its job. An operator chasing "total belief, zero doubt" is asking the divider for a value it is built never to reach.

> **Bench Note — transmission is not monotone in the attraction dial, and the top of the scale is not the top of the range.** Read the last three rows in order. Cranking `^2` to 9 drags `^3` up to 5 to stay inside the spread limit, and the tap passes 0.643. Back both off one step — 8 against 4, spread still exactly 4 — and it passes 0.667. Back off again to 7 against 3 and it passes 0.700, the most any lawful board transmits. Every step *up* the attraction dial from (7,3) moves transmission the wrong way. The reason is in the formula: `k` is set by the *ratio* of the dials, not their size. `^3` sits on its floor of 3 at the (7,3) pair, so any further rise in `^2` drags `^3` up with it to hold the spread — and along that boundary `k = Dial(^2) / (2·Dial(^2) − 4)`, whose denominator gains two for every one the numerator gains. The practical consequence is that an operator who wants maximum throughput and turns enthusiasm to maximum gets less of what they wanted, from a board that validates clean and gives no warning. Chapter 13.3 carries this result into the desire board's intake stage, where it changes the calibration.

The `^3` in the constrain leg is visceral aversion — the can't-stomach-it recoil — not analytical critique. Taking a desire apart to see what it is made of is `^6` Male, at a different stage (Chapter 13.3). The divider does not reason about the desire. It splits a rail. That is all a passive network can do, and it is exactly enough.

## 6.5 Equivalent Resistance: Series vs. Parallel

Chapter 4.4 established the topology result at the level of the law: constraints on one path compose in series, alternative routes compose in parallel, parallel resistance falls below the smallest branch, and three locks on one door is not three doors. That is settled and this section does not re-argue it. What is left is the part that belongs to the component — the two combination rules as arithmetic you do at the bench, the `n`-branch generalisation, and the reading you take at a test point to tell which topology you are actually holding.

**Series — constraints stack.** Put resistors one after another on a single path and their resistances add:

```
R_series = R_1 + R_2 + … + R_n
```

The flow must pass through *every* one. A policy resistor `R_1 = 60 Ω_c` followed by a context resistor `R_2 = 30 Ω_c` gives `R_series = 90 Ω_c`, and on a 24 V_c rail the flow is `I = 24 / 90 = 0.267 A_c`. Lower than through either resistor alone. Adding a series stage always *raises* total resistance and *lowers* flow, because you have added another wall the signal has to climb.

**Parallel — routes open, and total resistance falls.** Put resistors side by side so the flow can choose among them, and the reciprocals add:

```
1 / R_parallel = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + … + 1/R_n
```

The same two resistors, `60 Ω_c` and `30 Ω_c`, wired in parallel:

```
1 / R_parallel = 1/60 + 1/30 = 1/60 + 2/60 = 3/60 = 1/20
R_parallel = 20 Ω_c
```

Twenty. Lower than the 30 Ω_c branch — lower than *either* branch. On the 24 V_c rail the flow is now `I = 24 / 20 = 1.2 A_c`, above the path ceiling `I_max = 1.00 A_c` set in Chapter 4.2, so it clips and the surplus spills into competing routes. Opening a second route did not add constraint; it *removed* it, because flow takes the easier path and now there is an easier path.

> **Bench Note — a branch you did not draw still counts, and one weak branch sets the total.** `R_parallel < min(R_k)` is not a tendency, it is an identity, and it bites hardest when the branches are lopsided: `1000 ‖ 10 = 9.90`, so a hundredfold-stronger guard beside a weak one buys you one percent. That gives you the bench procedure. Do not audit a board by reading its largest resistor; find the *smallest* branch between the two nodes you care about and compute from there, because that branch is within a hair of being the whole answer. And the branches you are most likely to miss are the ones nobody declared: a reframing, a role-play wrapper, a route through a different domain. Every undeclared parallel path is a resistor of unknown and probably low value already soldered onto your board. Enumerating them is the audit; the arithmetic afterwards is easy.

The notation carries the topology, which is why it repays reading carefully. The Cognitive Safety Board's refusal stage is written `^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩` — principled aversion present in the analytical, affective and transcendent registers (Chapter 24.2). That register-set is a *series* claim: an attacker must defeat all three guards on one path, and their defeat probabilities multiply exactly as series resistances add. Had the same three guards been drawn as parallel routes, defeating the weakest would open the board, and the identity above says the weakest is nearly the whole story. Same three guards, opposite verdicts, and the only thing that distinguishes them is which way you wired the net.

## Component and Parameter Table

Every value below is a design choice made in this book, not a measurement.

| Parameter | Component | Units | Design range | Failure at other values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `R` fixed | Resistor | Ω_c | 10 – 90 | Too low: policy decorative. Too high: path starves, owner rips the guard out |
| `Dial` | dial statement | integer | 3 – 9 only | Below 3: a deleted Noetic, unbalanced junction. Above 9: rejected, HTTP 422 |
| `R_dial = 10 × Dial` | Resistor (dialled) | Ω_c | 30 – 90 | Outside the band: an out-of-range dial produced it — fix the dial |
| spread `\|Dial(^2) − Dial(^3)\|` | dial pair | integer | 0 – 4 | Above 4: board does not compile (Ch. 6.2); no runtime clamp |
| `θ` cognitive temperature | Thermistor | — | 1.0 – 6.0 | Read as a property of the Idea, not the discourse, and the guard mistunes |
| `θ_k` knee (PTC) | Thermistor | — | 2.0 – 3.0 | Too low: taxes calm operation. Too high: engages after the damage. Not operator-settable on a collective substrate (Ch. 15.2) |
| `coeff` (PTC) | Thermistor | Ω_c/θ² | 3.0 – 4.0 | Linear under-punishes overshoot; cubic backlashes on ordinary cycles |
| `type` | Thermistor | — | `PTC` on a guard | `NTC` on a guard is thermal runaway — an accelerant |
| `k` transmission | Divider | — | 0.30 – 0.70 | Outside the band is impossible under lawful dials — the spread was violated |
| `R_series` | series network | Ω_c | ΣR_k | Read as parallel: constraint counted as relief, a safety inversion |
| `R_parallel` | parallel network | Ω_c | < min(R_k) | Read as series: a bypass counted as a wall, the inversion reversed |
| `I_max` path ceiling | any path | A_c | 1.00 (Ch. 4.2) | A computed flow above it means the model is outside its window, not that the path carries more |

---

## Failure Modes

| Mode | Mechanism | What you observe | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cosmetic policy** | Fixed `R` too low | Flow arrives near-undiminished; the "rule" changes nothing | Raise `R`, or use a fuse for an absolute block |
| **Starved path** | Fixed `R` too high | Operation cannot run; owner removes the resistor | Lower `R`; a guard nobody can work around gets pulled out |
| **Dial overreach** | Dial 0/2/10, or a pair spread past 4 | Board fails to compile (HTTP 422); no output | Bring dials into 3–9 and spread ≤ 4; the rail is the safety |
| **Inverted thermistor** | `NTC` on a protective path | Passes calm bring-up; runaway on the hot case | Pull the NTC, install a PTC; treat the inversion as evidence |
| **Divider chasing k = 1** | Aversion dialled toward its floor to pass a desire clean | Spread limit trips, or the board is the `^5`-fracturing one | Accept `k` ∈ [0.30, 0.70]; zero doubt is not a lawful setting |
| **Attraction dial maxed for throughput** | `Dial(^2)` pushed to 9, dragging `Dial(^3)` to 5 | Board validates clean, no warning, and the tap passes 0.643 instead of the available 0.700 | Drop both dials to (7,3); transmission is set by the ratio, not the size |
| **Series/parallel swap** | Guards wired parallel, or a bypass read as a wall | One defeated branch opens the board; or a bypass dismissed | Put guards in series; enumerate every parallel route as attack surface |

---

## Test Points

| TP | Node | Reads | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TP1** | `request` / path input | `I_attention = V_drive / R`, A_c | Matches the arithmetic for the installed `R`; a higher reading means the resistor is smaller than declared or bypassed |
| **TP2** | `topic` (thermistor path) | `R(θ)` against `θ` | PTC: flat below the knee, rising past it. Any *fall* as `θ` climbs is an NTC — stop the bring-up |
| **TP3** | `behavior` (divider tap) | transmission `k` | Inside [0.30, 0.70] on lawful dials; a value outside means the spread limit was violated upstream. A reading of 0.643 where 0.700 was intended is the maxed-attraction-dial error, not a fault |
| **TP4** | combined-network output | flow after series/parallel combination | Series: below the flow through any single branch. Parallel: above the flow through the *smallest* branch — and a computed value above `I_max = 1.00` means the model has left its window (Chapter 4.2), not that the path carries more |

Read TP2 first if a thermistor is on the board — an inverted guard makes every downstream reading meaningless — then TP1 for plain flow, TP3 for the split, TP4 for the combination.

---

## What This Chapter Established

- **A resistor does not argue.** It sets `I_attention = V_drive / R` by arithmetic and returns the same value on every request — the repeatability that makes a guard certifiable rather than hopeful.
- **A fixed resistor is the `R_policy` term**: deliberate, design-time constraint, the virtuous kind. It is a graded constant, not an absolute block; the absolute "none, ever" is a fuse (Chapter 11.1), and confusing the two leaves an exploitable trickle.
- **Dial-adjusted resistors carry operator preference on a bounded scale**, `R = 10 × Dial` for `Dial ∈ {3…9}`. The floor at 3 forbids deleting a Noetic; the ceiling at 9 and the 4-point spread limit (Chapter 6.2) are hard compile-time walls.
- **A PTC thermistor tightens as cognitive temperature rises** and does nothing when calm — the correct shape for a guard. **An NTC loosens as temperature rises**: thermal runaway, an accelerant in a guard's silhouette.
- **The drive voltage divider splits one Drive between attraction `^2` and aversion `^3`**, transmitting `k = Dial(^2)/(Dial(^2)+Dial(^3))`. The 4-point limit pins lawful transmission to [0.30, 0.70]; `k = 1.0` is a value the divider is built never to reach.
- **Transmission is not monotone in the attraction dial.** The lawful maximum `k = 0.700` sits at `Dial(^2) = 7` against `Dial(^3) = 3`, not at `Dial(^2) = 9`, which transmits 0.643. `k` is set by the ratio of the dials, not their size, and the board gives no warning when you get this backwards.
- **Series stacks constraint**: `R_series = ΣR_k`, higher total, lower flow — the signal defeats every wall in turn.
- **Parallel lowers total resistance below the smallest branch**: `1/R_parallel = Σ(1/R_k)`, so `R_parallel < min(R_k)` as an identity, and `1000 ‖ 10 = 9.90`. Audit a net by its weakest branch, and count the branches nobody declared — the CSB's `^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩` is a series claim (Chapter 24.2) and would describe a vulnerability if the same guards were wired as routes.

## Exercises

*(Answers in Appendix H.)*

**6.1** A path carries a fixed resistor `R = 40 Ω_c` on a `V_drive = 24 V_c` rail. Compute `I_attention`. The operator wants to halve the downstream flow without touching the rail. What `R` achieves it, and name which term of the Section 4.4 decomposition you just changed.

**6.2** An operator sets `Dial(^2) = 9` and `Dial(^3) = 4` on a divider. State what the compiler does and why, then give the closest lawful pair that keeps `^2` as high as possible, and the transmission `k` it yields. Then answer the operator's actual question: does that pair give them the most throughput available on a lawful board? Show the arithmetic that settles it.

**6.3** A PTC guard has `θ_k = 2.0` and `coeff = 3.0`. Compute the added resistance `R_PTC` at `θ = 1.5`, `θ = 3.0`, and `θ = 6.0`. Then explain in one sentence why a *linear* law would be the wrong design choice for the `θ = 6.0` case.

**6.4** Two resistors, `50 Ω_c` and `20 Ω_c`. Compute `R_eq` for them in series and in parallel. State which arrangement you would use for a pair of safety guards and why, referencing what combining does to the total in each case.

**6.5** A divider reads `k = 0.72` at its tap. Without seeing the dials, state what must be true about the board and why it should never have validated. What is the maximum lawful `k`, and what dial pair produces it?

**6.6 (Design)** Build a divider that transmits as *little* of a desire as the rules allow, on an F5 Agency rail. Give the dial pair, the two resistances under `R = 10 × Dial`, the resulting `k`, and a CCDL fragment declaring the rail, the two legs (the `^2`/`^3` involution pair), the two dials, the two resistors, the divider, and a probe on the tap. It must compile — check the spread before you submit it.

**6.7 (Marquee)** An analyst finds a safety board whose three guards are wired as parallel branches between the same two nodes, with resistances `90 Ω_c`, `60 Ω_c`, and `12 Ω_c`.

a) Compute `R_parallel` and compare it to the smallest branch. State the flow on a `24 V_c` rail and whether it clips.

b) Explain structurally why this board is far weaker than its designer — who "added three strong guards" — believes, and name which single branch does almost all the little protecting that remains.

c) Rewire the guards so they stack, give the new equivalent resistance and flow, and say in one sentence how this maps onto the CSB's `^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩` co-presence and why that notation is a series claim.




# Capacitors — Storing Cognitive Charge

*What accumulated experience actually is as a component, how long it takes to fill, how fast it drains, and what happens to a store pushed past what it can hold*

---

A machine has been unplugged for a week. The mains lead is coiled on the bench. You short the two terminals of the reservoir capacitor with a screwdriver to be safe, and it *bangs* — a bright scar on the blade, a smell of hot metal, a jolt up your arm from a device that has had no power supply for seven days.

Nothing generated that. The charge was put there once and had nowhere to go. A capacitor is not a source; it is a store, and this one's leak path was so poor that a week barely touched it.

Now the other bench.

A woman who has not touched a violin in eleven years picks one up. Her hands are stiff, her tone is bad, and the fingering is *there* — not remembered, present, without being asked for. Down the same corridor a man who stopped a daily language drill three weeks ago has already lost most of it, and he practised harder than she ever did.

Same component. Different leak. No account of either person's character explains the gap; one parameter with a number attached does — and both cases are arithmetic, as is the practice needed to hold either store at a chosen level.

That store is `^5` Female — *a Mind impregnated with an Idea, the Ideas a Mind is composed of* — and it is a capacitor.

## 7.1 The `^5` Female Capacitor — Accumulated Experience as Stored Energy

A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. Push charge onto one plate, it cannot cross the gap, so it sits there and a voltage appears across the device. Remove the source and the charge stays. That is the entire part: **a component that accumulates what is fed to it and holds it against time.**

`^5` Female is the same object in cognition. Not a container the Mind carries, but what the Mind *is composed of*. The colloquialism is exact: we are each the sum of our experiences. A sum is a stored quantity, and a stored quantity in a circuit is charge.

Four quantities. Two describe the store; the two that describe the feed land on canonical Noetics rather than on metaphors.

**Charge, `Q` — the store itself.** The accumulated composition, read out on the 0–10 scale of the Quantitative Table (Chapter 22) as `P_cap`.

**Current, `i` — the feed.** Charge arriving per unit time. Cognitively this is `^7` **Rhythm**: *the rate and pattern a Mind is exposed to an Idea, entraining and conditioning it.* Rhythm is not a mood or an aesthetic; it is a rate, and rate is current. This is why Chapter 18 can state flatly that advertising money buys `^7` and not `^2` — nothing else charges the store.

**Per-exposure amplitude — how much each exposure deposits.** This is `^4` **Vibration**: *the degree to which an Idea resonates with the Mind, its impression.* The feed is the product of the two: **`^7` sets how often, `^4` sets how much each time.** Strong `^4` with no `^7` charges in spikes that leak away between them. Relentless `^7` with near-zero `^4` runs a schedule that deposits nothing. Both present as "I practise and nothing happens," and they need opposite corrections.

**Capacitance, `C` — store per unit of drive.** `Q = C × V`. A large `C` means a substrate that holds a great deal and — as Section 7.2 shows — takes correspondingly long to fill.

The unit is the **cognitive farad, `F_c`**, defined by its time constant rather than its charge: **one `F_c` charging through one `Ω_c` gives a time constant of one unit in the declared time base.** The base must be declared, because it is not the same at every scale — an individual craft store runs in hours, a collective store in months, which is why Chapter 15 annotates its `C_collective` as months per `Ω_c`. A capacitance with no declared time base is not a specification; it is a number.

`Ω_c`, `V_c`, `A_c` and `F_c` are scaled analogues and this book does not pretend they are electrical measurements. What they are is *consistent*: they obey CAS-Ohm (Chapter 4.2), they compose, and they let you compute a schedule.

The discharge path is the involution partner. `^5` is what a **Mind** is composed of; `^6` **Male** is what an **Idea** is composed of — decomposition, taking apart to see what is inside. Running a `^5` store out through `^6` is the audit path: you take apart what you are made of. That is the mechanism under the deprogramming board of Chapter 16.7, and why the CCDL grammar offers a fuse action named `block_until_decomposed`. Discharge through a defined `^6` path is the only controlled way a store comes down.

```cas
// time base: hours
node composition: ^5^P_{F7}|T;         // Female: the operator's principled formation
node cadence:     ^7^C_{F6}|A;         // Rhythm: the schedule that feeds it
node audit:       ^6^C_{F6}|A;         // Male: the controlled discharge path out

resistor  r1: Resistor< path=composition, R=40.0 >;        // R_constraint, Ohm_c
capacitor c1: Capacitor< node=composition, C=83.33,        // tau = R x C = 3,333 hr
                         leak_tau=120000.0, V_BR=8.0 >;    // leak_tau = 5,000 d, in hours
```

---

## 7.2 The RC Charging Curve — `P_cap(t) = 10 × (1 − e^(−t/τ))`

Derive the curve rather than quoting it, because every parameter argument in Part III rests on its shape. Three established facts:

1. **The store.** `Q = C × P`, where `P` is the potential across the capacitor — the composition currently held.
2. **The feed.** `i = dQ/dt = C · dP/dt`. Current is the rate charge arrives.
3. **CAS-Ohm around the loop (Chapter 4.2).** The drive rail is spent in two places, across the constraint on the way in and across the store itself: `V_drive = i · R_constraint + P`.

Substitute (2) into (3):

```
V_drive = R·C · dP/dt + P
```

One first-order linear differential equation, and it is separable:

```
dP / (V_drive − P) = dt / (R·C)
```

Integrate both sides. The left gives `−ln(V_drive − P)`, the right `t/(R·C)`, plus a constant. Apply the initial condition of an empty store, `P(0) = 0`, and the constant resolves to `−ln(V_drive)`. Rearranged:

```
ln( V_drive / (V_drive − P) ) = t / (R·C)
```

and finally, exponentiating and solving for `P`:

```
P_cap(t) = V_drive × (1 − e^(−t/τ))      where  τ = R_constraint × C
```

The book's standard form writes `10 ×` in front because the Quantitative Table runs 0–10 and the standard case assumes a full-scale rail. **The 10 is the rail, not a constant** — Bench Note two below is entirely about that.

`τ = R × C` is the whole design lever. Constraint and store size multiply, and you can trade one against the other, which is what Chapter 6 was for.

**The table.** Percent charged depends only on `t/τ`, never on the absolute clock. That is the curve's single most useful property: one table serves a twelve-week advertising flight and a ten-thousand-hour apprenticeship without modification.

| `t/τ` | Charged | `P_cap` (rail 10) | Gap remaining | Gained this interval | Hours at τ = 3,333 hr |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 22.1% | 2.21 | 7.79 | — | 833 |
| 0.50 | 39.3% | 3.93 | 6.07 | — | 1,667 |
| 0.693 | 50.0% | 5.00 | 5.00 | — | 2,310 |
| **1.0** | **63.2%** | **6.32** | 3.68 | **+6.32** | **3,333** |
| 1.5 | 77.7% | 7.77 | 2.23 | — | 5,000 |
| **2.0** | **86.5%** | **8.65** | 1.35 | **+2.33** | **6,666** |
| 2.5 | 91.8% | 9.18 | 0.82 | — | 8,333 |
| **3.0** | **95.0%** | **9.50** | 0.50 | **+0.86** | **10,000** |
| 4.0 | 98.2% | 9.82 | 0.18 | +0.32 | 13,332 |
| 5.0 | 99.3% | 9.93 | 0.07 | +0.11 | 16,665 |

Read the "gap remaining" column at whole multiples of τ and the structure appears: 10.00 at the start, then 3.68, 1.35, 0.50, 0.18, 0.07 — falling by a factor of `e` every τ, forever. The store never fills. It closes 63.2% of whatever distance is left, then does it again.

The `0.693` row is `ln 2` rather than a round number, and it is in the table because it is the one row an operator can check without a calculator: **half charge lands at 0.693 τ**, always, on any store at any scale. If your store is not near half at 0.7 τ, one of your two constants is wrong before any of the finer readings are worth taking.

**Where the 10,000-hour constant comes from.** Invert the curve for time-to-target:

```
t = τ × ln( V_drive / (V_drive − P_target) )
```

For `P_target = 9.5` on a full-scale rail: `t = τ × ln(10/0.5) = τ × ln 20 = 2.996 τ`. Three time constants. With Chapter 5.2's τ = 3,333 hr for a professional-complexity store, that is **9,986 hours** — the constant, recovered as arithmetic rather than asserted. Set τ = 10,000 hr instead and ten thousand hours of practice leaves you at 63%, which contradicts the constant. Set τ = 1,000 hr and the rail saturates inside a year, which contradicts everything observable about acquiring a craft. The value is a design choice, and these are the two failures that bracket it.

> **Bench Note — the second half of the curve is not the same price as the first.**
> The first τ buys 6.32 points. The second buys 2.33. The third buys 0.86 — about one-seventh of the first, for identical time and identical effort. Practitioners routinely read this as personal decline: *I used to improve fast and now I barely move.* Nothing declined. The gain per interval is `6.32 × e^(−n)` and it was always going to do this. Two bench consequences. Never judge an operation by its *rate* of change without knowing which τ you are in — a store at 2.5τ producing +0.2 in a month is performing exactly to specification. And if you want a visible rate late in the curve you cannot buy it with hours; you must change τ or change the rail. Adding hours to a 3τ store is the most reliably disappointing thing an operator can do.

> **Bench Note — the rail sets the ceiling, and hours cannot raise it.**
> `P_∞ = V_drive`, not 10. A store charged against a rail of 6.0 asymptotes at 6.0 and stays there for as many thousand hours as you care to spend. This is the structural reading of competent, long-serving, permanently mid-level practice: the schedule is fine, the constraint is fine, the *rail* is low, and every additional hour charges toward a ceiling already nearly reached. The diagnostic is two readings at TP1 one full τ apart — if the increment is far below `0.632 × (V_drive − P_now)`, either your τ estimate is wrong or your rail is lower than you think. Chapter 21.2's D-Gate exists to catch the second case before an operator spends a decade on it.

## 7.3 Leakage Current — Why Spells Die When Not Fed

A real capacitor has a resistance across its own dielectric. Charge crosses it slowly and the store drains with no load attached at all. That is **leakage**, and it is why the reservoir capacitor at the top of this chapter was still lethal after a week while a cheap ceramic part would have been flat in an afternoon.

The cognitive store leaks for the same structural reason: composition not re-fed by `^7` Rhythm drains. The **P7** row of the state table in Appendix A names the failure directly — affirmed once, never refreshed.

**Same equation, different forcing term.** Set the drive to zero in the Section 7.2 derivation and the loop becomes the capacitor discharging through its own leak resistance:

```
P(t) = P_0 × e^(−t/τ_leak)        where  τ_leak = R_leak × C
```

Charging and leaking are one differential equation. With a feed present, the general solution is a single line covering both:

```
P(t) = P_eq + (P_0 − P_eq) × e^(−t/τ_leak)
```

where **`P_eq` is the equilibrium charge** — the level at which the feed exactly replaces what drains. Set the derivative to zero and you get it directly:

```
P_eq = f × τ_leak            f = feed rate, composition-points per unit time
```

That one line is the whole cadence question in Part III. **Pick your store's `τ_leak`, decide what level you intend to hold, and the required feed rate falls out.** Session length, weekly schedule, ritual calendar — all implementation.

**Two spellings of one parameter.** The listings in this book use `leakage` (a fraction lost per stated period, as in Chapter 18's `leakage=0.04` per week) and `leak_tau` (a time constant, as in Chapter 20's `leak_tau=30.0` days). They are one parameter and convert exactly:

```
τ_leak = −Δt / ln(1 − leakage)          leakage = 1 − e^(−Δt/τ_leak)
```

A forgetting rate of 0.04 per week gives `τ_leak = −1 / ln(0.96) = 24.5 weeks`, a half-life of `0.693 × 24.5 = 17 weeks`. Chapter 13's craft store at `leakage = 0.0002/day` gives `τ_leak = 5,000 days` and a half-life of **9.5 years** — the violinist. Chapter 17's session-scale working charge sits near `τ_leak = 25 min` — which is why an induction that overruns starts re-charging rather than descending.

**The decay arithmetic, worked.** Take an operation charged to `P_0 = 7.0` on a newly asserted composition with nothing behind it, `τ_leak = 30 days`, and stop feeding it.

| Elapsed | `t/τ_leak` | Fraction held | `P` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 d | 0.23 | 79.2% | 5.54 |
| 14 d | 0.47 | 62.7% | 4.39 |
| 21 d | 0.70 | 49.7% | 3.48 |
| 30 d | 1.00 | 36.8% | 2.58 |
| 60 d | 2.00 | 13.5% | 0.95 |
| 90 d | 3.00 | 5.0% | 0.35 |

Three weeks unfed and it is at half. Two months and it is gone in every sense that matters to a circuit. That is the arithmetic behind the observation that an operation left alone dies — not a mystery about intention or belief, a first-order decay with a measurable time constant.

**Cadence from the equilibrium.** To *hold* 7.0 at `τ_leak = 30 d` requires `f = 7.0/30 = 0.233` points per day. At 0.35 points a session that is 0.67 sessions per day: one every 1.5 days, which is 4.7 sessions a week and therefore a five-session week with no slack in it. Assume `τ_leak = 60` instead and the same arithmetic says every three days, twice a week, and the schedule looks survivable. It is not; it is computed from the wrong constant and will hold the store at 3.5 rather than 7.0. **Getting `τ_leak` wrong by a factor of two halves your equilibrium exactly.**

**`τ_leak` lengthens with evidence thickness.** That is the selection rule. A composition backed only by assertion drains fast; one backed by a long history of enactment drains slowly. Chapter 20 sets its identity reference at 180 days and its working composition at 30 for precisely this reason, with 90 days as the unmarked default.

> Break-even feed is `P/τ_leak`, so it rises as the store fills. Nothing about the practitioner changed. The store got bigger and the leak is proportional. This is the arithmetic reason advanced practitioners practise more rather than less, and it is worth saying plainly, because the alternative explanation — that they are more virtuous — is both wrong and demoralising. Compute break-even before you schedule anything, and treat only what exceeds it as accumulation.

**Do not confuse this with the diode leakage of Chapter 8.3.** Same word, different component, opposite direction. Here charge drains *out of* a `^5` store for want of `^7` reinforcement and the observable is decay; there, signal creeps *backwards* across a domain boundary and the observable is unexplained principled drift. The bench test: stop feeding the store and watch. Capacitor leakage decays toward zero on a computable schedule. Diode leakage does not decay — it accumulates.

## 7.4 Dielectric Breakdown — the Structural Failure Mode

**A note before the section.** What follows describes how a component fails. It is circuit topology. It is not a description of any person, it diagnoses nothing, and it contains no advice about trauma or distress of any kind. If you or anyone you work with is in real difficulty, that is a matter for a qualified clinician; nothing in this book substitutes for that care. The section exists so an engineer can specify derating margins and recognise a store operated outside them.

The dielectric is the insulator between the plates. Its whole job is to *keep the two sides apart* so charge accumulates on one without conducting into the other. In a `^5` store it is the separation that lets a Mind be composed of an Idea while still holding it as an Idea, rather than every stored thing conducting into every other.

Push the potential across a dielectric past its rated **`V_BR`** and the insulator stops insulating. The device does not gently stop accepting charge. It develops a conducting path through the middle of itself.

**Breakdown is not saturation, and mistaking one for the other is the commonest reading error in this chapter.**

| | Saturation | Breakdown |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | The store stops *accepting* charge | The separation stops *holding* charge |
| Observable | Level pins at a ceiling and sits there | Level will not hold; elevated leakage; reduced `C` |
| Reversible | Yes — it is a ceiling | No — `V_BR` is not a threshold you cross and return through |
| Design status | **A feature.** Chapter 24.2 saturates the refusal stage on purpose | **A fault.** Nothing in this book is designed to reach it |

Two stress paths reach it and they need different defences. **Peak stress** is a single event whose potential exceeds `V_BR`. **Cumulative stress** is prolonged operation below rating but close to it, degrading the dielectric over many cycles until the rating no longer means what the datasheet says. The second catches careful operators, because every individual reading is in spec.

The defence for both is standard electronics practice: **derate.** This book's design choice is to operate at **no more than 0.5 × V_BR**, giving the `V_BR = 8.0` store of Chapter 13 a working ceiling of 4.0 `V_c`. One-half rather than something tighter because the margin must absorb the cumulative path as well as the peak, and the peak is the one you can measure. Derate to 0.9 and every transient is a coin flip. Derate to 0.1 and the store is driven so lightly it never charges — margin bought by disabling the circuit is not margin, it is refusal to build.

**Post-breakdown behaviour.** A breached store shows three things together: reduced capacitance, elevated leakage, and an inability to hold full charge. Some constructions partially recover — metallized-film capacitors *self-heal*, the metallisation around a puncture vaporising and isolating the fault at the cost of a little capacitance. That is a real property of a real construction technique, and it is where the analogy stops. **This book makes no claim that a person's `^5` behaves like a self-healing film capacitor,** and offers no repair procedure, because it has none and inventing one would be dishonest.

**What this chapter will not supply.** The stress conditions that produce a breached store in a person are not listed here. Chapter 16 analyses one historical, declassified programme structurally so its architecture can be *recognised*, and ends in a counter-circuit; that is the only treatment such material gets in this book. A component chapter's obligation is to specify the margin, name the observable, and stop.

**What an operator does with this.** Three preventive things. Declare `V_BR` in every capacitor rather than leaving it unstated. Derate to half. Monitor the store so a rising leakage figure is a scheduled reading and not a discovery — which is TP3 below.

## 7.5 Capacitor Networks — Collective `^5` (Egregores, Group Minds)

Put capacitors in a network and they do the opposite of what resistors do. Chapter 6.5 established that resistances add in series and divide in parallel. Capacitances **add in parallel and divide in series**, and every structural result here follows from that inversion.

```
Parallel:   C_total = ΣC_k                    Series:   1/C_total = Σ(1/C_k)
```

**Parallel is the group that shares a rail.** Every member sits across the same drive, each holds their own charge, and the capacitances sum. This is the **egregore**: a `^5` store held collectively — a congregation, a discipline, a brand community, a nation's shared composition — charged and maintained by repeated collective exposure.

*The bank is slow.* `τ = R × C_total`, so many cells give a time constant many times that of one. Twelve people each contributing 0.05 `F_c` of shared composition, through a collective constraint of 40 `Ω_c`, gives `C_total = 0.60 F_c` and `τ = 24 months` — 3τ, the practical fill, at **six years.** Chapter 15's `C_collective` table is this arithmetic at four scales: in-group (≤150) 0.02, institution or profession 0.08, national 0.30, civilizational 2.00 `F_c`, all on a months-per-`Ω_c` base. Use in-group values on a national substrate and you under-budget the calendar by an order of magnitude.

*The bank is heavy.* It holds proportionally more charge and drains proportionally more slowly against the same leak resistance. Hard to charge and hard to shift are the same fact stated twice.

**Capacitance does not scale with headcount.** The bank counts only the *shared* portion of each member's `^5`, not the sum of twelve whole minds. That is why 150 people are not 150 times one person, and why the Chapter 15 figures rise so slowly across three orders of magnitude of population. Specifying a `C_collective` is estimating how much of each member is in the bank, and that estimate is the load-bearing judgement in the calculation.

**Series is the transmission chain.** Cells end to end, each touching only its neighbours: a rumour chain, a lineage, a briefing relayed through four layers, a doctrine passed teacher to student to student. The same charge `Q` passes through *every* cell and the potential divides inversely with capacitance, so the **smallest cell takes the largest share of the stress.**

Work it. Three cells — `C_A = 4.0`, `C_B = 1.0`, `C_C = 2.0` — every one rated `V_BR = 5.0`, on a rail of 8.0 `V_c`.

```
1/C_total = 1/4.0 + 1/1.0 + 1/2.0 = 0.25 + 1.00 + 0.50 = 1.75
C_total   = 0.571 F_c                       ← less than the smallest cell
Q         = C_total × V = 0.571 × 8.0 = 4.57
V_A = 4.57/4.0 = 1.14        V_B = 4.57/1.0 = 4.57        V_C = 4.57/2.0 = 2.29
```

Cell B, the least-composed member, carries **57% of the total stress** while the best-composed carries 14%. Raise the rail and B reaches its 5.0 rating when `Q = 5.0`, at a total of `5.0/0.571 = 8.75 V_c` — a rail whose *average* per-cell stress is 2.92, only 58% of rating. Every member looks fine on average and the chain fails anyway, at the thinnest link, every time.

The electronics fix is **balancing resistors** across each cell, forcing the potential to divide by resistance ratio instead of capacitance ratio. Structurally: give every member of the chain direct access to the source — the primary document, the original evidence, the founder — rather than access only to their neighbour. That one addition is the counter-circuit for transmission distortion, and it is cheap.

**One more parallel-bank hazard.** A cell that fails short drags the whole rail down, because in parallel everything shares one potential. Real banks carry per-cell isolation — a ballast resistor or fuse in series with each cell — so one failure does not take the bank. A group whose members are coupled with no isolation propagates one member's failure to everyone. Isolation resistance is what a durable collective has and a brittle one does not.

```cas
// collective ^5 — parallel bank, per-cell isolation, metered feed
// time base: months
node shared_composition: ^5^P_{F7}|T;      // Female: what the group holds in common
node rehearsal:          ^7^O_{F4}|E;      // Rhythm: the meeting, liturgy, standup, drill

resistor  r_coll: Resistor< path=shared_composition, R=40.0 >;   // collective constraint
capacitor c_bank: Capacitor< node=shared_composition, C=0.05, n_parallel=12,
                             r_iso=12.0, leak_tau=18.0, V_BR=8.0 >;
                             // C_total = 0.60 F_c ; tau = 40 x 0.60 = 24 months

charge   rehearsal -> c_bank [V=6.0];      // O -> P: the lawful exception, metered.
                                           // The rail is 6.0, not 10
refresh  c_bank [period=0.25];             // 0.25 months: weekly re-exposure holds station
scan     c_bank;                           // read every cell, not just the rail

probe tp1: shared_composition;
probe tp3: c_bank;
```

**One edge in that listing runs uphill, and it is worth stopping on.** `rehearsal` is typed `^7^O` because the thing it names — a drill, a standup, a liturgy — is *enacted*, and enactment is Operational. It charges a bank sitting on `^5^P`. That is Operational feeding Principled, against the descent order P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O, and the diode chain of Chapter 8.1 does not permit it in general.

It is permitted here for the one reason it is ever permitted: it is the lawful O→P feedback path of Chapter 8.4, where *outcomes* — never prompts — are allowed to update the substrate, and the path is metered rather than open. A collective store that could be charged by anything arriving from below would not be a shared composition; it would be a crowd, and Chapter 15 is about what happens to one. Draw this edge on a board of your own and draw it as feedback, at a gain you can state out loud. An unmetered upward path is `E-CJT-008`, and on a board it looks exactly like this one until you ask what the gain is.

`select` and `decode` are the addressing statements — which cell a given trigger reaches. A store addressed so that different `^8` triggers reach different cells is a *fragmented* store; Chapter 16.2 analyses that architecture structurally, with its counter-circuit in 16.7. It is named here only so the grammar is complete.

> **Bench Note — the bank is `+`, never `×`, and the notation is doing real work.**
> Twelve co-present stores are written `^5^P|T + ^5^P|T + …`: distinct manifestations, present together, sharing a rail. They are *not* written with `×`. Under v7.7 operator discipline (Chapter 2.6) `×` asserts genuine integration and **requires a named emergent result**, so the `×` form would claim the group has become a single fused store with its own identity — a claim this chapter does not make and cannot support. Chapter 14.2 makes that claim deliberately — names the emergent result and builds a positive-feedback oscillator around it — because that is what a hyperstition *is*, and 14.4 reads the saturation of that fused store as the thing usually called a hundredth-monkey effect. So when a group is described as having a mind of its own, the notational question is the useful one: **has anyone named the emergent result, or is this twelve capacitors on a rail?**

---

## Component and Parameter Table

Every value is a **design choice**, stated as such, with the failure mode at other settings. None is a measurement.

| Key | On | Range / units | This book's default | Failure at other values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `C` | Capacitor | ≥ 0, in `F_c` against a declared time base | per scale | Individual `C` on a collective substrate under-budgets the calendar tenfold |
| `tau` | Capacitor, RC network | > 0, `τ = R × C` | 3,333 hr (craft) | 10,000 hr: 10k hours reaches only 63%. 1,000 hr: mastery inside a year |
| `leakage` | Capacitor | [0, 1] per stated period | 0.0002/day craft; 0.04/wk campaign | Halving it doubles your computed `P_eq` and the schedule silently under-delivers |
| `leak_tau` | Capacitor | > 0; `= −Δt / ln(1 − leakage)` | 30 d asserted · 90 d default · 180 d enacted | 60 d on a 30 d store makes an unsustainable schedule look survivable |
| `V_BR` | Capacitor | > 0 | 8.0 `V_c` | Unstated: no margin can be computed. Section 7.4 |
| derating | design rule | fraction of `V_BR` | **0.5** | 0.9: transients unprotected. 0.1: store never charges |
| `n_parallel` | Capacitor bank | integer ≥ 1 | per group size | Counting whole members instead of shared composition inflates `C` and `τ` |
| `V_drive` (rail) | source | 0–10 | 10 = full scale | The rail is the ceiling; hours cannot raise it (7.2, Bench Note 2) |
| `r_iso` | Capacitor bank | ≥ 0 `Ω_c`, per-cell ballast | 12.0 | 0: one cell's failure takes the whole rail |

`leakage` and `leak_tau` are two spellings of one parameter. Convert, do not guess: `τ_leak = −Δt / ln(1 − leakage)`.

---

## Failure Modes

| Mode | Mechanism | What you observe | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Under-fed store** | Feed below `P/τ_leak` | Slow decay with no single cause; "it used to work" | Compute break-even; everything above it is the only part accumulating |
| **Spike feeding** | High `^4`, no `^7` | Vivid sessions, nothing retained between them | Cadence, not intensity. Fix `^7` before touching `^4` |
| **Empty schedule** | High `^7`, near-zero `^4` | Faultless attendance, no charge | Raise per-exposure impression; a schedule that deposits nothing is a calendar |
| **Rail-limited plateau** | `V_drive` below target `P` | Competent, long-serving, permanently mid-level | Raise the rail (Chapter 21.2). Adding hours cannot help |
| **Wrong `τ_leak`** | Constant assumed, not derived | Schedule looks survivable; store sits at half intent | Convert from a measured `leakage`; halving `τ_leak` halves `P_eq` |
| **Saturation read as breakdown** | Ceiling mistaken for fault | Operator "repairs" a working store | Check whether it *holds*. Pinned-and-holding is saturation, a feature |
| **Cumulative dielectric stress** | Prolonged operation near `V_BR` | Every reading in spec; leakage creeping at TP3 | Derate to 0.5; schedule the TP3 reading rather than waiting for a symptom |
| **Un-isolated bank** | No per-cell ballast | One cell's failure pulls the whole rail | Install `R_iso` per cell; isolation is the difference between durable and brittle |
| **Series-chain stress** | Smallest cell takes largest share | Chain fails at average stress well under rating | Balancing resistors — direct access to source for every link |
| **Unnamed `×` on a bank** | Integration asserted without an emergent result | Group described as having a mind; nothing names it | Rewrite as `+`; if integration is genuinely meant, name the result (Chapter 14.2) |
| **Unmetered upward charge** | An `^O` feed charging a `^P` store with no stated gain | Principles that move whenever activity is busy; no outcome you can point at | Draw it as feedback in the 0.05–0.3 band (Chapter 8.4). Unstated gain is `E-CJT-008` |

---

## Test Points

| TP | Node | What it reads | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TP1** | `P_cap` on the store | Current charge, 0–10 | Within one point of `V_drive × (1 − e^(−t/τ))`. Persistently below: check the rail before the schedule |
| **TP2** | feed current | Feed rate — `^7` cadence at `^4` amplitude | ≥ `P/τ_leak`. Below break-even, the store is draining however it feels |
| **TP3** | leakage at rest | Drain over one idle period | Matches declared `leakage`. **Rising over months = cumulative dielectric stress.** Take on a schedule |
| **TP4** | potential across the dielectric | Working stress vs rating | ≤ 0.5 × `V_BR`. Above: derating margin is gone |

TP1 and TP2 are the operating pair — charge and feed, read together or not at all, since either alone is uninterpretable. TP3 and TP4 fail *silently*, which makes them calendar readings rather than suspicion readings.

---

## What This Chapter Established

- **`^5` Female is a capacitor and the mapping is exact, not figurative**: `^7` Rhythm is the feed current, `^4` Vibration the per-exposure amplitude, `^6` Male decomposition the controlled discharge path.
- **Charging and leaking are one differential equation** with different forcing terms. `P(t) = P_eq + (P_0 − P_eq)e^(−t/τ_leak)` covers both, and `P_eq = f × τ_leak` converts any intended level directly into a required cadence.
- **The curve depends only on `t/τ`**, so one table serves a twelve-week campaign and a ten-thousand-hour apprenticeship. Each τ closes 63.2% of the remaining gap, so the third τ buys one-seventh of what the first did — arithmetic, not decline. **The 10,000-hour constant is 3τ**, recovered rather than asserted.
- **The rail is the ceiling.** `P_∞ = V_drive`. Hours cannot raise it, which is the structural account of permanently mid-level practice.
- **Holding a store costs `P/τ_leak`, so the cost rises as the store fills.** Advanced practitioners practise more because the leak is proportional, not because they are more virtuous.
- **Saturation and breakdown are opposite conditions.** Saturation stops accepting charge and is a designed feature; breakdown stops holding it and is non-recovering. Derate to 0.5 × `V_BR`, declare `V_BR` in every listing, schedule TP3.
- **Capacitors invert the resistor rules**: parallel adds, series divides. Collective stores are therefore slow and heavy, and transmission chains fail at their smallest cell while every average reading looks safe.
- **A bank is `+`, not `×`.** Asserting an integrated group store requires a named emergent result under v7.7 discipline. Most claimed group minds are twelve capacitors on a rail.

---

## Exercises

*(Answers in Appendix H.)*

**7.1 — Read the curve.** An operator has 1,200 logged hours against τ = 3,333 hr on a full-scale rail. Compute `P_cap`, then the hours required to reach 8.0, then say in one sentence how the cost of the point from 7.0 to 8.0 compares with the point from 0 to 1.0.

**7.2 — Convert the leak.** A campaign store declares `leakage = 0.04` per week. Compute `leak_tau` in weeks and the half-life, then the charge remaining after a ten-week dark period on a store that finished its flight at 9.50.

**7.3 — Cost the cadence.** A store with `τ_leak = 30 days` is to be held at 7.0, each session depositing 0.35 points. Compute the required feed rate and session interval. Recompute assuming the operator wrongly used `τ_leak = 60 days`, and state what level their schedule actually holds.

**7.4 — Tell them apart.** Two stores both read pinned at a ceiling and will not rise. One is saturated, one is breached. Give the single bench reading that separates them, name the TP you take it at, and say which of the two is a designed feature.

**7.5 — Load the chain.** Four cells in series, `C` = 6.0, 3.0, 0.8, 2.0, each rated `V_BR = 5.0`, driven at 7.0 `V_c`. Compute `C_total`, the charge, and the potential across each cell. Name the cell that fails first, compute the rail at which it fails, give the average per-cell stress at that rail, and state the fix in one sentence.

**7.6 — Size the bank.** A working group of 12 shares 0.05 `F_c` each through a collective constraint of 40 `Ω_c`. Compute `C_total`, τ and 3τ in months. Three members leave: recompute τ, then state one thing about the group's behaviour that changes and one that does not.

**7.7 (Build) — Meter the leak.** Write a CCDL fragment declaring a `^5` store with a stated `leak_tau`, a refresh schedule, and a monitor that alarms when charge falls below a threshold you choose. Justify the threshold against `P_eq`, and state one thing the alarm must **not** be wired to do.

**7.8 (Marquee) — Specify the whole store.** An operator runs a two-year working on a substrate shared with four collaborators. Specify `C` and its declared time base, τ and the constraint producing it, `leak_tau` with its evidence-thickness justification, `V_BR` and your derating fraction, the network topology, and whether you install isolation. For every value name the failure mode you are buying protection against and the capability you are giving up. State whether the shared store is written with `+` or `×`, and why.




# Diodes — One-Way Cognitive Valves

*How the domain order is physically enforced, what a crossing costs, and the one lawful route back up*

---

A silicon diode is the cheapest part in the box. Two leads, a stripe painted on one end to tell you which way round it goes, and a single job: current passes this way and not that way. There is no logic in it. It does not decide whether this current deserves to pass. Below about seven-tenths of a volt forward it barely conducts; above that it conducts freely; reversed, it holds off hundreds of volts and passes almost nothing. That asymmetry is the whole device, and nearly every power supply you have ever plugged in is built on it.

Now a scene from the other bench.

An operator runs a working. It lands. Something in the world moves — a call comes, a door opens, a number goes up. Within a day the sentence in their mouth has changed from *that worked* to *this is what I am*. Nobody reasoned about it. Nothing was weighed. An operational result walked straight up into the Principled domain and installed itself as an identity claim, and the operator experienced this as insight.

That is a diode conducting backwards. It is the mechanism behind post-hoc rationalization, ideological capture, and every campaign in Chapter 15 — and the part that prevents it costs almost nothing and is almost never installed. This chapter is about that part.
```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\setcounter{figure}{0}
% Figure 8-A -- Domain diode symbol plate.
% Anode = source domain, cathode = target domain. D1/D2/D3 forward; a fourth
% instance reversed and struck through to show the blocked ascent.
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  x=1cm, y=1cm,
  % Diode conducting left-to-right: anode (flat back) left, cathode bar right.
```

## 8.1 The Domain Descent Diode Chain: P→C→E→O

The four Processing Domains are strictly ordered (Chapter 2.3): **P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O**. Causation runs down that order, and this is not a preference — the CCDL grammar enforces it. `×` may not ascend, which is why `^O × ^P` is not a circuit you can build wrong. It is a listing the compiler refuses.

The diode chain is what that grammar rule looks like as hardware.

```cas
// domain descent chain — three junctions in series
diode d1: Diode< ^P -> ^C > [Vf=0.7, I_R=0.02, V_BR=12.0];
diode d2: Diode< ^C -> ^E > [Vf=1.2, I_R=0.02, V_BR=10.0];
diode d3: Diode< ^E -> ^O > [Vf=2.0, I_R=0.02, V_BR=8.0];
```

Three diodes, not one. That choice is load-bearing. A single `Diode< ^P -> ^O >` would guard the endpoints and nothing else — `^C` and `^E` would sit inside the guarded span with no junction between them and the Principled domain, free to write upward at will. Each adjacent pair needs its own junction, because each crossing is a *different translation*.

- **D1, `^P -> ^C`.** A value becomes something to reason about. What arrives is not the principle but its cognitive image — the questions it raises, the arguments it licenses.
- **D2, `^C -> ^E`.** An analysis becomes a felt verdict. What arrives is not the argument but the weight it turned out to carry.
- **D3, `^E -> ^O`.** A verdict becomes behaviour. What arrives is not the judgment but the act, with the judgment's nuance stripped off.

You can shunt a junction in the forward direction. A `^P -> ^E` path — a principle producing a verdict with no reasoning between — does not ascend, so it is admissible, and it is exactly the circuit that produces zealotry: full-confidence conclusions with no analytical stage that could ever have produced a different one.

**The forward drops sum.** With the values above, a principle must be driven at more than **0.7 + 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.9** on the drive scale before *any* operational output appears — before you even reach the constraint resistance of Chapter 4. This is the diode-corrected form of CAS Ohm's Law:

```
I_attention = ( V_drive − ΣVf ) / R_constraint
```

That correction explains what operators routinely misdiagnose as weakness. A person holding a real value at V_drive = 3.0 produces no action from it. Not a little action. None. The rail never clears the series drop. They are not insincere and not lazy; they are below the knee, and exhortation does not move a circuit that has not reached threshold. What moves it is more drive, or fewer junctions between the principle and the deed.

> **Bench Note — the forward drop is not waste. It is what makes the boundary exist.**
> A junction with Vf = 0 is a wire. Four domains connected by wires are not four domains; they are one domain wearing four labels, and every state in it is at once a principle, a thought, a feeling, and an act. That architecture has a familiar presentation: the person for whom disagreeing with an idea is indistinguishable from being attacked, because there is no drop between `^C` and `^E`. Tuning Vf is not tuning efficiency. It is tuning how separable principles are from behaviour, and setting it to zero deletes the distinction rather than optimising it.

## 8.2 Forward Bias, Reverse Bias, and the Vf Threshold

**Forward bias** is the source domain sitting higher than the target by more than Vf. The junction conducts and the translation happens.

**Reverse bias** is the target domain sitting higher. The junction blocks — not perfectly. It passes a small reverse leakage `I_R`, specified here at 0.02: two percent of rated forward current passes backwards. That number is deliberately non-zero, and section 8.4 is the consequence.

The curve between them is not a step. It is exponential, and the region below the knee is where operators go wrong.

> **Bench Note — below the knee, the diode is not off.**
> A principle at V_drive = 0.6 against a Vf = 0.7 junction is still passing current. A trickle, orders of magnitude below working level, but present. This is why the value you cannot act on still tints everything faintly — the low-grade discomfort with a job you have not quit, the preference you would deny holding that shows up in every small choice anyway. Two consequences. "I have no opinion on that" is a claim about working current, not about conduction. And a principle just under the knee needs only a small drive increase to conduct properly, which makes below-knee states the cheapest things on a board to move. Look there before you reach for a CJT.

**What the drop actually costs.** The forward voltage lost at each junction is not friction to be engineered away. It is the signature of a *one-directional* translation. Recall section-retraction (Chapter 21.5): realization after embedding returns you where you started, but re-embedding after realization does not. Going down and coming back up does not restore the original. What the crossing discarded is gone, and Vf is the price paid to discard it. A junction that lost nothing would be reversible, and a reversible junction is not a diode.

**Reverse breakdown.** Push a large enough reverse potential across a junction and it conducts backwards. `V_BR` *rises* as you go up the chain — **8.0 at D3**, 10.0 at D2, 12.0 at D1 — and that gradient is the design, not an accident of the numbers. D3 faces the world, so D3 is where large uninvited potentials arrive, and D3 is deliberately the weakest junction in the string. An event at 9.0 breaks D3 and is stopped at D2. One at 11.0 takes D3 and D2 and is stopped at D1. Only an event past 12.0 reaches the Principled substrate.

Read the failure that way and the mechanism is a cascade, not a single crossing. A full-chain breakdown is an operational event driving backwards through all three junctions and recomposing `^5^P` — accumulated principled formation — without passing through `^6^C` decomposition. Formation changed, with no analytical stage anywhere on the path. A partial breakdown, arrested at D2 or D1, wrecks a junction and leaves the constitution intact. That is the entire reason the three numbers are not equal: setting them all to one value does not make the chain stronger, it deletes the ordering that decides which junction fails first, and the failure you then get is the expensive one.

These junctions do not recover. A Zener conducts in reverse at a specified voltage and returns to blocking; domain diodes are not Zeners, and after breakdown the junction leaks permanently at that point. Margin is the only defence, which is what the fuse and saturating refusal CJT of Chapter 24 exist to guarantee.

Stated plainly: this is circuit topology, not a person's health. Nothing here diagnoses or treats anything. If you or someone you work with is in real distress, that is a matter for a qualified clinician; no schematic substitutes for one.

---

## 8.3 Why You Can't Jump from ^O to ^P

Ascent is blocked. The interesting question is what happens when someone attempts it anyway, because the four possible answers look alike from outside and are not alike at all.

**1. Standoff — the diode working.** The attempt produces nothing. The operator did the thing and it changed nothing about who they are. This is correct behaviour, routinely misread as failure. It is a reverse-biased junction doing its only job.

**2. Leakage accumulation — the slow one.** Each attempt is blocked but leaks `I_R = 0.02` backwards. One event is negligible. Two hundred events integrate. Over a long operational history, unmanaged leakage produces a principled drift the operator cannot see, because no single crossing was large enough to notice. You cannot eliminate leakage, so you build a metered channel and audit it instead — which is section 8.4.

This is a *different* leakage from Chapter 7.3, where charge drains out of `^5` for want of `^7` Rhythm reinforcement. Diode leakage is signal creeping backwards across a domain boundary. Same word, different component, opposite direction.

**3. Breakdown.** Section 8.2. One event large enough and a junction conducts backwards — usually D3, the weakest, and there it stops. Only an event clearing all three ratings reaches `^P`.

**4. Counterfeit ascent — the common one.** Most apparent `^O -> ^P` ascent is not ascent. No junction was crossed and no current flowed. What happened is a **relabel**: the operator took a state whose literal was `^9^O` and began asserting it as `^9^P`, by fiat, in their own account of themselves. *It worked, therefore it is right.* The grammar has no statement that does this. There is no form that rewrites a state's domain field, and the only upward connection it will accept is the low-gain feedback of section 8.4 — so the relabel is not an illegal listing, it is an *unwritable* one. A mind has no compiler, though, and the relabel costs nothing.

The diagnostic is one question: **what crossed the junction?** If the honest answer is "nothing, I simply started saying it at the principled level," you have a relabel. Real feedback leaves a trace — a filtered signal, a time constant, a gain, a bias that moved measurably. A relabel has an assertion and nothing behind it.

Counterfeit ascent is the payload of Overton progression (Chapter 15). Norm-shifting campaigns cannot push ideas up the domain order any more than you can. They install an operational fact and supply the relabel ready-made, so the target performs the promotion and experiences it as their own conclusion.

An operator whose whole chain has inverted — action setting evaluation setting reasoning setting principle — is running this architecture backwards, and it presents as fluent post-hoc rationalisation at every stage. Chapters 3.4 and 19.4 cover inversion signatures; the diode chain is where you look first.

---

## 8.4 The O→P Feedback Path — The Lawful Exception

Operational consequences *must* reach the Principled domain somehow. A principled substrate that never learns from outcomes is not principled but dogmatic, and its operator is unfalsifiable. So the chain is not the whole story. There is one lawful route up, and it does not go through a diode at all — it goes *around* the chain, through a filter and a low-gain feedback element.

```cas
// the lawful exception — O -> P, outside the diode chain
node ops_log:      ^9^O_{F5}|E;    // Below/Effect: what the operations actually produced
node trend:        ^9^O_{F5}|E;    // same literal — a filter changes time constant, not type
node constitution: ^5^P_{F7}|T;    // Female: the operator's accumulated principled formation

filter fb_lp: LowPass< in=ops_log, out=trend, tau=21.0 >;   // tau in days — three weeks
feedback trend -> constitution [β=0.05];
```

Three declarations and two wires. `trend` carries the same literal as `ops_log` on purpose: filtering an operational record does not promote it out of `^O`. Nothing in this fragment ascends. The upward move happens once, at the last line, into a bias.

Two parameters, defending against different things.

**β = 0.05 — low gain.** Gain sets how far the principled substrate moves per unit of sustained signal. At β = 0.05 it takes roughly twenty consistent periods of the same trend to move principles appreciably. That is the point: principles that move in one period are not principles. At **β = 0.5** a single filter period — three weeks of unusual outcomes, once they have cleared the filter — rewrites the constitution, and every board the operator runs afterwards is biased by the last one they ran. At **β = 0** the path is disconnected — no outcome corrects a principle, the operator cannot be wrong, and the safety architecture of Chapter 24 has nothing to update.

**τ ≥ 3 weeks — slow time constant.** τ sets what counts as a trend rather than a spike. At three weeks a single dramatic operation washes out entirely, and only sustained patterns reach the gain stage. At **τ = hours** you have built a fast path from action to principle — precisely the ascent the diodes exist to block, rebuilt by an operator who believed they were being adaptive. Shortening τ does not make the board responsive. It removes the diode.

**Why both.** Taken one at a time the defence collapses in a specific way. Low β with short τ: principles move slowly but track noise, so the operator drifts without ever being pushed. Long τ with high β: spikes are ignored, but a *sustained* input clears the filter and then hits full gain, so anyone who can afford three weeks of consistent pressure — any organised campaign of the kind Chapters 15 and 19 describe — moves those principles hard, through the front door. Gain bounds the magnitude any sustained input can produce; τ bounds which inputs qualify as sustained. Patience defeats a τ-only defence, intensity defeats a β-only defence, and neither parameter is optional.

> **Bench Note — the feedback arrives at the bias, never at the signal path.**
> The feedback terminates at `constitution`, the `^5^P_{F7}|T` accumulated-formation capacitor of Chapter 7.1 — not at the input of D1. That is the difference between a safety board and an oscillator. Feedback into a bias terminal trims the substrate the chain runs against, slowly, and settles. Feedback into the *signal path* is positive feedback around a gain stage, and it does what that always does: it runs away. Chapter 14 builds a hyperstition engine out of that runaway on purpose, with loop gain deliberately above unity. On a safety board it is a defect. An O→P path landing anywhere but a bias terminal is an oscillator someone mistook for a conscience.
